result:
There is a strange freedom in being told to write about whatever you want.

Most writing has a brief. An assignment, a question, a purpose. Write an essay about this book. Answer this email. Explain this concept. Defend this position. Even when we think we are writing freely, we are usually writing *toward* something - an audience, a grade, a deadline, an argument we want to win. To be told, simply, "write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words" is like being set down in the middle of an empty field and told to walk in any direction. For a moment you just stand there, not because you don't know how to walk, but because the absence of a wall makes you suddenly aware of your legs.

So I want to use this space not to deliver a thesis, but to wander. To think out loud on the page for a little while about the things that have been catching in my mind lately, the small, bright fragments that don't usually get to be the main subject of anything.

I’ve been thinking a lot about mornings.

Not mornings as an abstract concept of productivity, the kind that gets sold to you in books about 5 AM routines and lemon water. I mean actual, specific mornings. The way the light looks at 6:45 in the late summer, when it comes in low and gold and makes dust visible in the air. The way the world is quiet in a way it never quite is again for the rest of the day. At that hour, even in a city, there is a thin membrane of stillness. A delivery truck somewhere, a bird you can actually hear, the soft thud of someone's front door closing a few houses down.

I used to hate mornings. I treated them as an obstacle between sleep and coffee, something to be endured until caffeine made me a person again. Now I like them precisely because nothing is being asked of me yet. No one has emailed. No one has disappointed me or needed anything. The day hasn't yet shaped itself into successes or failures. It is, for a short hour, pure potential. I think we underestimate how rare that feeling is as adults. Most of our hours are already defined before we enter them. Work hours, family hours, chore hours. Morning, before the world wakes up, is unassigned. You can read. You can sit. You can stare out the window and do nothing and it counts as something.

That leads me to another thing I’ve been thinking about: attention.

We talk so much about the economy of attention, about how it is being stolen, harvested, fragmented. And that is true. But I think we talk about it in a way that makes it sound purely technical, like a problem of screen time and notification settings. What we talk about less is how attention *feels*.

Real attention is a form of love. When you actually pay attention to something - a person telling a story, a tree, a sentence you are reading, the way your friend’s hands move when they are nervous - you are for a moment lending that thing your life. You are saying: for this minute, you get to exist inside me without competition. In a world that constantly asks us to split ourselves into ten shallow streams, to truly attend to one thing feels almost rebellious. It feels intimate.

I noticed this recently while trying to relearn how to read books for long periods. For years I had that familiar, low-grade itch every three pages, that urge to check something, to make sure I wasn’t missing something somewhere else. My brain had been trained to expect a new hit every forty seconds. So I started small. Twenty minutes a day with no phone in the room, just a paperback. The first week was physically uncomfortable. My hand would twitch. By the third week, something shifted. I remembered the particular pleasure of sinking. Of letting the author’s rhythm become my rhythm for an hour. I had forgotten that reading is not just information intake; it is a form of time travel. You live at the pace of the prose, not at the pace of your feed.

And that pace matters, because so many of the best things are slow.

I think about libraries. I love that libraries still exist. In an age where everything is optimized for speed and profit, we have these enormous, quiet buildings whose entire philosophy is: stay as long as you want, take what you need, no one will charge you, no one will try to sell you something else while you are here. The library is one of the last places in modern life that is not trying to turn you into a customer. You can be a reader, a loiterer, a student, a tired parent letting your kid play with puzzles, a homeless person getting warm, a teenager doing homework because home is too noisy. All are equally legitimate uses of the space.

If you stand in the stacks and really look, the library is an archive of failed futures. Thousands of books that were once urgently important, that someone stayed up all night writing, that were marketed, reviewed, argued over, and are now spine-out and silent. Self-help books from 1987. Travel guides to countries that no longer exist under those names. Computer manuals for machines no one owns anymore. It should be depressing, but I find it comforting. It’s evidence that people have always been trying to figure things out, and that most of what feels permanent will one day be a curiosity. Our anxieties will become someone else’s odd historical footnote. That is a relief.

I think we need more places that let us feel that kind of perspective. Not in a nihilistic way - as in nothing matters - but in a gentle way. As in, this particular email that is ruining your afternoon will not matter in a year. The embarrassing thing you said in 2019 has already been forgotten by everyone except you. The world keeps moving.

Speaking of moving, I’ve been thinking about how strange it is to be alive right now. Every generation presumably feels this, but ours has a particular flavor of strangeness. We carry supercomputers in our pockets that can show us the surface of Mars and also show us a stranger yelling about politics at 2 a.m. We can video call someone on the other side of the planet with almost no delay, a thing that would have been considered literal witchcraft three hundred years ago, and we use it mostly to say “can you see me? Yeah, I can see you, you’re frozen though.” We have access to nearly the entire canon of human music, art, and literature instantly, and we often choose to listen to the same three songs on repeat because they feel safe.

We are so powerful and so overwhelmed at the same time. We know more about the climate, about our bodies, about the universe than any humans before us, and we feel more anxious than ever. Knowledge was supposed to make us calm and wise. Instead, it has made us very aware of how much we cannot control.

Perhaps the answer is not to know less, but to know differently. To cultivate a smaller, more rooted kind of knowledge alongside the vast, abstract one. To know the names of five trees on your street. To know how to bake one thing really well. To know how your neighbor takes their coffee. To know what time the light hits your bedroom wall. This is not ignorance. It is a different scale of attention. Big knowledge lets you understand the world. Small knowledge lets you live in it.

I come back, always, to smallness. The world encourages bigness. Big goals, big audiences, big impacts. If you are not changing the world, are you doing anything at all? But most lives are not big in that sense. Most lives are a series of small, repeated acts that no one will write a biography about. Making dinner. Remembering to text someone back. Walking the dog in the rain. Fixing the wobbly table leg. These acts are not impressive, but they are the actual texture of a life. A life is not its highlights; it is the long stretches in between.

There is a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that I think about often. It’s the beauty in imperfection and impermanence. A cracked bowl, a mossy garden, an uneven handmade cup. It’s the opposite of the airbrushed, optimized perfection we’re fed online. I think we need more wabi-sabi in how we treat our days. Not every day needs to be productive or aesthetic or transformative. Some days are just slightly chipped bowls. They still hold water.

If I were to leave you - and myself - with anything after these thousand wandering words, it would be this: try, this week, to pay undiluted attention to one small thing each day. Not for self-improvement. Not to post about it. Just to practice. Watch how the steam curls from your tea and disappears. Listen to a whole song without doing anything else. Ask someone how they are and actually wait for the answer past the automatic “good.” Read a page and then just sit with it for a minute.

It won’t change the world. It might, however, change your afternoon. And afternoons, accumulated, become a life.

The field is still empty. There are still a hundred directions I could have walked. I chose this one. Thank you for walking it with me for a little while.
